verifyNote: Written from standard UK ocular pharmacology teaching, the BNF, NICE guidance and College of Optometrists guidance. Medicines law, exemptions, product licences and guidance change: always check the current BNF, the College's Clinical Management Guidelines and your lecturer's slides before relying on a dose or legal detail.

topics.title: How eye drops reach their target
topics.summary: Only a small fraction of an eye drop gets into the eye. Most overflows or drains down the nasolacrimal duct, where it can be absorbed into the blood. To cross the cornea a drug needs to dissolve in both fats (to pass the epithelium) and water (to pass the stroma). Understanding this explains dosing, side effects and why technique matters.
keyPoints: A typical drop is about 30–50 µl, but the eye holds only about 7–10 µl, so most of it is lost straight away.
Drainage through the nasolacrimal duct lets drugs reach the bloodstream through the nasal lining, bypassing the liver: this is how eye drops cause systemic side effects.
The corneal epithelium is lipophilic (fat-loving) and the stroma hydrophilic (water-loving), so the best drugs have both properties.
Closing the eyes or pressing on the inner corner (punctal occlusion) for 1–2 minutes increases absorption into the eye and reduces systemic absorption.
Darker irides bind some drugs to melanin, so dilation can be slower and sometimes needs more drops.
Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride keep multi-dose bottles sterile but can damage the ocular surface with long-term use.
examTraps: Assuming eye drops can't cause systemic effects: timolol drops can cause bronchospasm.
Giving two different drops one immediately after the other: the second washes out the first; wait about 5 minutes.
Forgetting that a damaged epithelium lets drugs (and toxicity) in much more easily.

diagram.description: A drop landing on the eye, with arrows showing: overflow onto the cheek, drainage through the punctum and nasolacrimal duct to the nose and bloodstream, and a small arrow passing through the cornea (epithelium, stroma, endothelium) into the anterior chamber. Add a finger pressing the inner corner to show punctal occlusion.

goDeeper.heading: Getting drops in well
goDeeper.body: Tilt the head back, pull the lower lid down, look up and put one drop into the pocket without touching the eye or lashes. Close the eye gently for 1–2 minutes (don't blink hard) and press the inner corner. Wait about 5 minutes between different drops, and put ointments in last. Many patients, especially older ones, struggle with technique, so show them and consider aids.

goDeeper.heading: Formulations
goDeeper.body: Solutions are quick but short-acting. Suspensions (for example some steroids) need shaking. Gels and ointments stay longer and are useful at night but blur vision. Preservative-free single-use vials suit patients using drops often, those with surface disease, and contact lens wearers. Pro-drugs (such as latanoprost) are changed into the active form inside the eye.

goDeeper.heading: Systemic absorption
goDeeper.body: Drug absorbed through the nose goes straight into the circulation without first passing through the liver. That's why a beta-blocker drop can slow the heart or tighten the airways, and why cyclopentolate can occasionally cause behaviour changes in small children. Punctal occlusion and using the lowest effective strength reduce the risk.

topics.title: Diagnostic drugs: mydriatics, cycloplegics, anaesthetics and stains
topics.summary: Optometrists use a small set of diagnostic drugs every day. Mydriatics widen the pupil to examine the fundus; cycloplegics relax accommodation for accurate refraction, especially in children; local anaesthetics numb the cornea for contact tonometry; and stains show damage to the ocular surface.
keyPoints: Tropicamide (0.5% or 1%): antimuscarinic mydriatic. Works in about 20–30 minutes, lasts around 4–6 hours, with only mild cycloplegia.
Phenylephrine (2.5%): sympathomimetic (alpha-1 agonist) that adds dilation; use with care in heart disease, high blood pressure and people taking MAOIs.
Cyclopentolate (0.5% under about 1 year, 1% in older children): the usual cycloplegic for children. Peak effect after about 30–60 minutes; can last up to 24 hours.
Local anaesthetics (proxymetacaine, oxybuprocaine, tetracaine, lidocaine with fluorescein) work within seconds and last about 15–20 minutes.

Fluorescein stains areas where the epithelium is missing and is used for tear break-up time, Goldmann tonometry and the Seidel test; lissamine green stains devitalised cells, especially on the conjunctiva.
Warn patients about blurred near vision and glare after dilation and advise them not to drive until their vision has recovered.
examTraps: Using tropicamide alone for a child's cycloplegic refraction: cyclopentolate is needed for full cycloplegia.
Forgetting to tell patients not to rub their eyes after anaesthetic drops (risk of corneal abrasion).
Not checking the angle (for example with Van Herick) and asking about risk before dilating.

diagram.description: An iris showing the circular sphincter (parasympathetic, muscarinic receptors) and the radial dilator (sympathetic, alpha-1 receptors). Arrows show tropicamide and cyclopentolate blocking the sphincter and ciliary muscle, and phenylephrine stimulating the dilator.

goDeeper.heading: Mydriatics versus cycloplegics
goDeeper.body: Antimuscarinics block both the iris sphincter and the ciliary muscle, so they cause dilation and cycloplegia; how much of each depends on the drug and strength. Tropicamide is short-acting with weak cycloplegia, ideal for fundus examination. Cyclopentolate gives strong cycloplegia for refraction. Atropine is the strongest and longest (days), usually used by hospital teams. Phenylephrine dilates without any cycloplegia.

goDeeper.heading: Cycloplegic refraction in children
goDeeper.body: Children have large amplitudes of accommodation that can hide hyperopia. Cyclopentolate (with or without tropicamide) relaxes accommodation so the true refractive error can be measured, usually by retinoscopy after 30–45 minutes. Side effects are rare but include flushing, fever, drowsiness or, rarely, hallucinations or unsteadiness; give parents written advice.

goDeeper.heading: Stains and what they show
goDeeper.body: Fluorescein glows green under blue light where the epithelium is broken (abrasions, ulcers, punctate staining) and in pooling under rigid contact lenses. A Seidel test uses concentrated fluorescein to show aqueous leaking from a wound. Lissamine green stains damaged or unprotected cells, useful for grading dry eye on the conjunctiva and lid margin, with less stinging than rose bengal.

checklist.title: Safe routine dilation
steps: Check history: previous dilation, heart problems, high blood pressure, medicines (for example MAOIs), allergies and pregnancy.
Assess the angle (Van Herick) and note risk factors for angle closure (hyperopia, older age, narrow angles).
Explain the purpose, effects (blur, glare) and that they shouldn't drive until vision recovers; get verbal consent.
Check the drug name, strength, expiry date and that the container is intact.
Instil the drop(s) and record drug, strength, number of drops, eye, time and batch number.
Re-check pupils and IOP if indicated after examination, and give written advice about warning symptoms (pain, redness, haloes).
Tell the patient to seek urgent help if they get a painful red eye or headache with haloes.

options.feedback: The standard cycloplegic for children over about a year.
Too weak a cycloplegic for this purpose.

mcq.explanation: Cyclopentolate is the routine cycloplegic for children.

options.text: Risk of a dangerous rise in blood pressure
options.feedback: MAOIs increase the pressor effect of sympathomimetics.
The concern is too much effect, not too little.

mcq.explanation: Sympathomimetic + MAOI can cause a hypertensive reaction.

mcq.q: After a penetrating injury, which test shows aqueous leaking from a wound?

options.feedback: Leaking aqueous dilutes the dye into a visible stream.
Used for surface damage, not leaks.

mcq.explanation: A positive Seidel test means a full-thickness wound: emergency referral.

cases.scenario: A 58-year-old with a history of heart disease is booked for routine dilation to examine diabetic retinopathy. His angles are open (Van Herick grade 3).
cases.question: Which drops would you use and what advice would you give?
cases.modelAnswer: Tropicamide alone (for example 1%) is usually enough and avoids the cardiovascular risk of phenylephrine. Explain blur and glare, advise him not to drive until his vision recovers, and tell him to seek urgent help for a painful red eye, haloes or headache. Record drug, strength, time and batch.

topics.title: Adverse reactions and contraindications, including angle closure
topics.summary: Every drug can cause harm. For diagnostic drops the key risks are triggering acute angle closure in a predisposed eye, allergic reactions, systemic effects and corneal toxicity from anaesthetics. Good history-taking, assessment of the angle and clear advice keep these risks low, and suspected reactions should be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
keyPoints: The risk of dilation triggering acute angle closure is low, but higher with hyperopia, older age, shallow anterior chambers, a family history and East Asian ethnicity.
Assess the angle (Van Herick, and gonioscopy if available) before dilating; mid-dilated pupils are the danger point.
Allergic reactions range from mild lid redness (often to preservatives or neomycin) to rare anaphylaxis.
Repeated or self-administered anaesthetic drops damage the corneal epithelium: never give patients anaesthetic drops to take home.
Systemic effects: beta-blocker drops (asthma, slow heart), phenylephrine (blood pressure), cyclopentolate (CNS effects in small children).
Report suspected adverse drug reactions to the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.
examTraps: Refusing to dilate anyone with a narrow angle without weighing benefit: sometimes dilation is essential, with precautions and advice.
Thinking pilocarpine after dilation prevents angle closure: it isn't recommended routinely and can make some situations worse.
Forgetting to record batch numbers, which are needed if a reaction occurs.

diagram.description: Two cross-sections of the anterior chamber. Left: open angle with aqueous flowing to the trabecular meshwork. Right: a mid-dilated pupil with pupil block, the iris bowing forward (iris bombé) and the peripheral iris blocking the meshwork, with an arrow showing IOP rising.

goDeeper.heading: Recognising acute angle closure
goDeeper.body: Symptoms: painful red eye, blurred vision, haloes around lights, headache, nausea or vomiting. Signs: a fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy (oedematous) cornea, shallow anterior chamber and very high IOP (often 50 mmHg or more). It's an emergency: arrange same-day assessment at the hospital eye service by phone, following local protocol.

goDeeper.heading: Taking a drug history
goDeeper.body: Ask about all medicines, including inhalers, eye drops, over-the-counter and herbal remedies, and recreational drugs. Ask about allergies and what happened. Note conditions that matter: asthma or COPD, heart problems, high blood pressure, pregnancy and breastfeeding. Check the BNF for interactions and contraindications.

goDeeper.heading: Yellow Card reporting
goDeeper.body: Any health professional, and patients themselves, can report a suspected adverse reaction to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme. Report serious reactions and any reaction to medicines marked with a black triangle (under additional monitoring). You don't need to be certain the drug caused it.

flashcards.front: Main risk factors for angle closure
flashcards.back: Hyperopia, older age, shallow AC, family history, East Asian ethnicity.

flashcards.front: Classic pupil in acute angle closure

options.feedback: This is an emergency needing same-day treatment.

options.text: Wait until the drops wear off tomorrow

mcq.explanation: Pain, haloes and vomiting after dilation = suspected acute angle closure.

topics.title: Medicines law for optometrists
topics.summary: UK medicines fall into three legal categories: General Sales List (GSL), Pharmacy (P) and Prescription Only Medicines (POM). All optometrists can use and supply certain medicines in their practice under exemptions in the Human Medicines Regulations 2012. Optometrists with extra qualifications can supply more (Additional Supply), prescribe as supplementary prescribers, or prescribe independently.
keyPoints: Categories: GSL (any shop), P (pharmacy, with a pharmacist), POM (normally needs a prescription).
All optometrists can sell or supply GSL and P medicines in the course of their professional practice.
Exemptions let all optometrists use certain POMs in practice (for example some diagnostic drugs) and supply a small list of POMs in an emergency; check the current list.
Additional Supply (AS) optometrists can supply a wider range of POMs, such as some anti-infectives.
Independent prescribing (IP) optometrists can prescribe any licensed medicine for conditions of the eye and surrounding tissue within their competence, except controlled drugs.
IP, AS and supplementary prescribing (SP) are specialist registrations with the GOC.
examTraps: Saying all optometrists can prescribe POMs: only IP (and SP within a management plan) can prescribe; others use exemptions.
Forgetting that IP is limited to the optometrist's own competence and to eye conditions.
Supplying a medicine without recording it properly.

diagram.description: A pyramid or ladder with three medicine categories (GSL at the bottom, P in the middle, POM at the top) and, beside it, the levels of optometric practice: all optometrists, Additional Supply, Supplementary Prescriber, Independent Prescriber, with arrows showing what each can access.

goDeeper.heading: What 'supply' means
goDeeper.body: Supplying a medicine means handing it to the patient (with or without charge) after an assessment, with clear labelling and instructions, and recording it. Optometrists' exemptions only apply in the course of professional practice and, for some POMs, only in an emergency. Wholesale supply or supplying for people you haven't examined isn't covered.

goDeeper.heading: Becoming a prescriber
goDeeper.body: IP training includes a College of Optometrists theory qualification, a period of supervised clinical learning with a designated medical practitioner or independent prescriber, and a final assessment, followed by GOC specialist registration. Newer MOptom degrees (for example the five-year courses with prescribing) are starting to build this in. IP optometrists often work in community services for minor eye conditions and in glaucoma clinics.

goDeeper.heading: Patient Group Directions
goDeeper.body: In some NHS services, optometrists can supply or give specified medicines under a Patient Group Direction (PGD): a written instruction, signed off by the service, for treating a defined group of patients without an individual prescription. PGDs are common in minor eye condition services. Each PGD lists exactly which drugs, which patients and what training is required.

flashcards.front: What is a PGD?

Most optometrists use exemptions, not prescriptions.
AS allows supply of a wider list, not prescribing.

Supply must be properly authorised in writing.

mcq.explanation: PGDs are widely used in NHS eye services.

topics.title: Anti-infectives, anti-allergy drugs and anti-inflammatories
topics.summary: Most eye infections and inflammations seen in practice are treated with a handful of drug groups: antibiotics for bacterial infection, antivirals for herpes simplex, anti-allergy drugs for allergic conjunctivitis, and steroids or NSAIDs for inflammation. Knowing when not to treat, and when a steroid could be dangerous, matters as much as knowing what to use.
keyPoints: Most acute bacterial conjunctivitis gets better on its own; a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol may speed recovery when it's severe or not settling.
Contact lens–related keratitis is an emergency because of Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba risk; it's usually managed in hospital with fluoroquinolones or other intensive treatment.
Herpes simplex dendritic ulcers are treated with an antiviral (for example aciclovir or ganciclovir), never with a steroid alone.
Allergic conjunctivitis: mast cell stabilisers (for example sodium cromoglicate) and antihistamines; dual-action drugs (for example olopatadine) do both.
Topical steroids reduce inflammation but can raise IOP, cause cataract and make herpes or fungal infections much worse.
Topical NSAIDs (for example ketorolac, nepafenac) are used for pain and inflammation, especially after cataract surgery.
examTraps: Using a steroid on an undiagnosed red eye: it can turn a herpes ulcer into a sight-threatening one.
Treating a contact lens ulcer as simple conjunctivitis.
Expecting a mast cell stabiliser to work straight away: it takes days and works best before exposure.

diagram.description: A flow chart starting at 'red eye'. Branches: bacterial conjunctivitis → often self-limiting, consider chloramphenicol; viral conjunctivitis → supportive care; allergic → mast cell stabiliser / antihistamine; herpes simplex keratitis → antiviral, refer per protocol; contact lens ulcer → emergency referral; anterior uveitis → urgent referral for steroid and cycloplegic.

goDeeper.heading: Antibiotics
goDeeper.body: Chloramphenicol is broad-spectrum and widely used for superficial infections (drops in the day, ointment at night). Fusidic acid works mainly against staphylococci and is used twice daily. Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are reserved for more serious infections such as keratitis. Overuse drives antibiotic resistance, so treat only when there's a clear benefit.

goDeeper.heading: Steroids
goDeeper.body: Topical steroids range from potent (dexamethasone, prednisolone acetate 1%) to milder or 'soft' (fluorometholone, loteprednol). They're used for uveitis, after surgery and for some severe allergic or immune conditions, usually under specialist care. Risks: raised IOP in 'steroid responders', posterior subcapsular cataract, delayed healing and worsening of infections. They're tapered rather than stopped suddenly after longer courses.

goDeeper.heading: Anti-allergy drugs
goDeeper.body: Mast cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglicate, lodoxamide) stop mast cells releasing histamine, so they are best started before the allergy season and take several days to work. Antihistamines (for example antazoline, azelastine) give quick relief of itch. Dual-action drugs (olopatadine, ketotifen) combine both. Cold compresses and avoiding the allergen help too.

flashcards.front: Why avoid steroids in an undiagnosed red eye?
flashcards.back: They can make herpes simplex or fungal infections much worse.

flashcards.front: Antiviral for herpes simplex dendritic ulcer
flashcards.back: Topical aciclovir or ganciclovir (usually managed per protocol/specialist).

flashcards.front: Two eye risks of long-term topical steroids
flashcards.back: Raised IOP and posterior subcapsular cataract.

flashcards.front: When should mast cell stabilisers be started?
flashcards.back: Before allergen exposure (they take days to work).

options.feedback: Suspected microbial keratitis needs urgent specialist care.

Stop lens wear and refer; don't refit now.

mcq.explanation: Contact lens keratitis is sight-threatening and needs emergency referral.

options.text: A topical steroid on its own
options.feedback: Steroids can make an epithelial herpes ulcer spread and deepen.

mcq.explanation: Never give steroids alone in active epithelial herpes.

options.text: Start a mast cell stabiliser a couple of weeks before the season
options.feedback: They prevent release of histamine but take time to work.

options.feedback: Not first-line; risks outweigh benefits for routine hay fever.

cases.scenario: A 30-year-old has had a sticky, red left eye for two days. No pain, normal vision, no contact lenses. There's a purulent discharge and the cornea is clear.
cases.question: How would you manage this?
cases.modelAnswer: Likely acute bacterial conjunctivitis, which is usually self-limiting. Advise lid hygiene, cleaning discharge, not sharing towels and handwashing. If severe or not improving after a few days, a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol can be supplied (within the optometrist's legal scope). Advise returning urgently if pain, photophobia or blurred vision develops.

topics.title: Glaucoma medicines
topics.summary: Glaucoma treatment lowers intraocular pressure, either by reducing aqueous production or by increasing outflow. Prostaglandin analogues are the usual first drop; beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists are added if needed. NICE now recommends laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) as a first-line option for many patients. Optometrists need to know side effects and contraindications to support patients.
keyPoints: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost, tafluprost): increase uveoscleral outflow, once a day at night. Side effects: red eye, longer darker lashes, darker iris, skin around the eye darkening, fat loss around the eye.
Beta-blockers (timolol, betaxolol): reduce aqueous production. Avoid in asthma/COPD, slow heart rate and heart block.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: drops (dorzolamide, brinzolamide) reduce production; oral acetazolamide is used short-term (tingling, tiredness, kidney stones, low potassium).
Alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine): reduce production and increase outflow; allergy is common; avoid in young children.
NICE NG81 recommends offering selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) as first treatment for ocular hypertension (at the treatment threshold) and chronic open-angle glaucoma.
Adherence is a major problem: forgetting drops, poor technique and side effects all reduce effectiveness.
examTraps: Forgetting that beta-blocker drops can cause asthma attacks or fainting.
Telling patients the iris colour change from prostaglandins will go away: it's usually permanent.
Assuming that once IOP is 'normal' the patient can stop drops.

diagram.description: Cross-section of the anterior eye with labels showing where each drug class acts: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-blockers and alpha-agonists on the ciliary body (reduce production); prostaglandin analogues on the uveoscleral route; pilocarpine and SLT on the trabecular meshwork (increase conventional outflow).

goDeeper.heading: Choosing and adding treatment
goDeeper.body: NICE NG81 recommends offering SLT first for many people with ocular hypertension or COAG; if drops are used, a generic prostaglandin analogue is usually first. If the target IOP isn't reached, treatment is stepped up: another class, a combination drop (fewer bottles helps adherence) or surgery. Preservative-free options are considered for surface problems.

goDeeper.heading: Side effects to watch for
goDeeper.body: Prostaglandin analogues: hyperaemia, eyelash growth, iris darkening (permanent), periorbital skin darkening and fat atrophy, and rarely cystoid macular oedema or uveitis. Beta-blockers: bronchospasm, bradycardia, tiredness, low mood. Brimonidine: allergic follicular conjunctivitis, dry mouth, drowsiness (and serious sedation in infants). Dorzolamide: stinging, bitter taste.

goDeeper.heading: Helping with adherence
goDeeper.body: Ask how patients use their drops and watch them do it. Simplify regimes, link drops to a daily routine (for example brushing teeth), use reminders and drop aids, and explain that glaucoma has no symptoms until late, so stopping drops is risky. Report suspected side effects to the prescriber rather than advising the patient to stop.

cases.scenario: A 68-year-old on latanoprost for two years says one eye now looks browner than the other and his lashes are longer. He wants to stop the drops.
cases.question: How would you respond?
cases.modelAnswer: Explain these are known effects of prostaglandin analogues: the lash growth may reverse if stopped, but iris darkening is usually permanent. Stress that stopping could let glaucoma progress without symptoms. Don't advise him to stop; check adherence and technique, record the findings and let his glaucoma clinician know his concerns so they can discuss alternatives.

topics.askClaude: Make a table of glaucoma drug classes with mechanism, example, main side effects and contraindications, then quiz me.

topics.title: Systemic medicines with eye side effects
topics.summary: Many medicines taken for other conditions affect the eyes. Some cause minor symptoms such as dry eye; others cause serious damage that needs screening, such as hydroxychloroquine retinopathy. Asking about all medicines in every eye examination helps spot these effects early.
keyPoints: Hydroxychloroquine (for lupus and rheumatoid arthritis): retinal toxicity; the Royal College of Ophthalmologists recommends screening after about 5 years of use (or after 1 year with extra risk factors), using OCT and visual fields.
Corticosteroids (tablets, inhalers, nasal sprays, creams near the eye): posterior subcapsular cataract and raised IOP.
Amiodarone: whorl-like corneal deposits (vortex keratopathy) and, rarely, optic neuropathy.
Tamsulosin and similar alpha-blockers: floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery (tell the surgeon).
Ethambutol (for TB): optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and colour vision.
Topiramate: can cause sudden bilateral angle closure and a myopic shift, usually in the first weeks of treatment.
examTraps: Only asking about eye drops when taking a drug history.
Forgetting that bilateral acute angle closure in a young person on topiramate is a drug reaction, not typical angle closure.
Mixing up which drug causes which effect.

goDeeper.heading: Hydroxychloroquine screening
goDeeper.body: Toxicity is related to daily dose by body weight and to how long the drug has been taken; risk is higher with kidney disease and with tamoxifen. Early damage shows on OCT as thinning of the outer retina around (or in some ethnic groups, further out from) the fovea, before patients notice anything. Damage is permanent, so screening aims to stop the drug before vision is affected. Follow the Royal College of Ophthalmologists' current recommendations.

goDeeper.heading: Other drugs to know
goDeeper.body: Antihistamines, antidepressants and antimuscarinics: dry eye and reduced accommodation. Isotretinoin (for acne): dry eye, meibomian gland problems and poor night vision. Sildenafil: temporary blue-tinged vision. Vigabatrin: permanent visual field constriction (fields monitored). Digoxin toxicity: yellow-tinted vision. Bisphosphonates: rarely uveitis or scleritis.

goDeeper.heading: What to do when you suspect a drug effect
goDeeper.body: Record the medicine, dose and duration, and examine carefully. Don't tell the patient to stop a medicine they need: write to the prescriber or GP, and refer urgently if vision is threatened (for example drug-induced angle closure or optic neuropathy). Report suspected reactions to the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.
